studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Let Hope Divert Them
studies.meaning: After the letters and a statement about the Book, a prediction: those refusing now will wish they had submitted. Commentators place that wish at death or at the reckoning, and the sources keep both. Then an instruction that sounds like release but is not, telling the messenger to leave them to eating, enjoyment and being diverted by long expectation. The final verse supplies the reason the instruction is safe to follow. No town was ever removed without a written term already set for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, opening a surah that will move quickly to the making of the human being and the refusal of Iblis. The audience was prosperous, and the message threatened arrangements that were working. Nothing here reports an occasion. The instruction to leave them alone belongs to a stage where argument had been offered repeatedly and was no longer producing anything new.

keyTerms.note: A particle grammarians read either as rarely or as often, and both readings are recorded. It occurs in only this one place in the whole Quran, which is why its force is discussed at such length.

Hope stretched over distance, the assumption that there will be time later. The definite form appears once in the Quran, here, and the classical tradition habitually sets it against the appointed term.
A written and known decree, the phrase occurring only here. Naming it as written removes any suggestion of improvisation, so the delay a person reads as safety is a term already fixed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long-range planning was how Meccan wealth was built. A merchant committed capital to a caravan that would not return for months, arranged marriages years ahead, and thought in seasons rather than days. That habit of mind is exactly what this passage names. Expectation of future time was not a weakness in that culture; it was the skill the whole economy ran on.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the phrases in these opening verses occur nowhere else in the Quran. The particle in the second verse appears only here, the definite word for long expectation appears only here, and the phrase for a known writ appears only here. Very few passages of this length contain that many terms unique to themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies distraction rather than argument as the real obstacle. Eating, enjoying and assuming there is time are not crimes, and none of them is named as one, but together they postpone the question indefinitely. Placing a written term behind the whole scene also changes what patience means for the one watching. Nothing is running late, because the schedule was never his to read.

crossReferences.why: Names the same distraction, abundance occupying people until they reach the graves.
States the fixed term for every nation, unable to be advanced or delayed by an hour.
Uses the only other occurrence of this word for hope, attaching it to lasting good deeds instead.

studies.applyIt: Notice the phrase later this year in your own thinking. The conversation you will have, the change you will make, the person you will visit. Pick the one that has been postponed longest and put a date on it in your calendar today. Long expectation is the specific thing this passage names, and a date is its opposite.

studies.title: We Send Them Only With Truth
studies.meaning: A rule about terms is followed by two quoted taunts and one short answer. No community outruns or delays its appointed span. Then the objectors call the recipient of the reminder mad and demand that angels be brought if he is truthful. The reply refuses the request by explaining what angels are for: they descend only with the settled matter, and once they do, no further waiting is granted. Commentators read this as saying the demand asks for the end of the reprieve rather than for evidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands for a visible angel are recorded in several surahs from this period, sometimes as a request for a companion warner alongside the messenger. Accusations of madness were the standard charge against anyone claiming unseen communication, since possession by spirits was the available explanation for such speech in that culture.

keyTerms.note: The word for remembrance and for what prompts it, used here by the objectors themselves for what was sent down. Even in mockery they name the message accurately, which is part of the passage's irony.
Built on the same root as the word for the unseen beings called jinn, so the accusation is literally that he is jinn-touched. It explains unusual speech by assigning it to an unseen source.
From the verb for looking and waiting, in a form meaning granted time. The same word appears later in this surah when Iblis asks for exactly this and receives it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had a recognised category for people who spoke from an unseen source. Soothsayers delivered rhymed oracles and were understood to have a jinn companion feeding them, and they were consulted and paid without being trusted. Calling a man possessed was therefore not merely an insult; it was placing him in a known professional slot, one his audience already knew how to discount.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran answers the demand for angels in several places and gives a different reason each time. One passage says that if an angel had been sent down the matter would have been settled with no reprieve; another that an angel sent to human beings would have had to be made a man, leaving everyone as confused as before; a third that angels are sent to those who live where the messenger lives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer treats the reprieve itself as the mercy being overlooked. Angels descending in the requested form would end the interval in which anyone can still change position, so granting the demand would cost the demanders everything. That reframes an unanswered request as a form of protection. It also states something about how the unseen operates: it does not appear on request, and its appearance would mean the matter is closed.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand, saying the matter would have been settled and no respite given.
Records the same request and describes what seeing the angels will actually mean for sinners.
Uses the same word for respite later in this surah, when Iblis asks for it and is granted it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have asked for that you are glad you did not receive on your own timetable. A job, a relationship, a confrontation. Notice that the delay was doing something. Then name one thing you are pressing for now, and consider what the interval before it might be for.

studies.title: The Reminder And Its Keeper
studies.meaning: The famous first line uses emphatic constructions three times over: We, and only We, sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardians. The commentators divide over the scope of the pledge, most reading it of the Quran and its preservation from loss or alteration, some extending it to the protection of the message and its bearer. The four ayat that follow explain why the pledge is needed, since mockery of messengers is presented as a pattern, not an accident.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when opponents were calling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) mad and demanding angels as proof, quoted three ayat before this passage. The pledge of preservation lands in the middle of that ridicule, when the community was small and the revelation existed mainly in memory and on scattered materials. No particular occasion is reported. The surah takes its name from a rock-cut settlement mentioned later in it.

keyTerms.note: One of the Quran's names for itself, from the root for remembering and mentioning. Calling revelation a reminder implies the content is not new information but something the hearer already owes.

A plural participle of guarding, used of watchmen, memorisers and anything kept intact. The same root gives the title for someone who holds the whole text in memory, which is one way the pledge has been carried.

A word for a beaten track that later travellers follow. Here it names the established pattern of how earlier peoples behaved and what happened to them, which is presented as evidence rather than as threat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Texts in that world were fragile things. Writing surfaces were bone, palm stalks, thin stone and scraps of leather, and a single fire or flood could take a library. What held a poem intact for a century was not parchment but a professional memory: reciters carried thousands of lines and were corrected in public if they slipped. A promise to preserve a text was a promise about people as much as about materials.
studies.didYouKnow: The pledge is given in the first person plural of majesty and repeated in the same breath, a doubling that Arabic uses for oaths. The wording does not say the Reminder will not be attacked; it says it will be guarded, which is a claim about outcome rather than about ease. The surah later mentions a valley whose rock-cut tombs still stand in northern Arabia.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches the survival of the text to God rather than to the community, which changes what preservation means. It is not presented as an achievement of scholarship or of memory, though both are how it happened, but as something undertaken from the other side. That places a limit on anxiety about the Quran's integrity, and it also places a limit on credit. And the ayat that follow refuse to treat rejection as a sign the message failed.

crossReferences.why: Says falsehood cannot approach the Book from any side, the same guarantee stated negatively.
Assigns the gathering and the reciting of the revelation to God, not to its receiver.
States the same pattern of mockery: no messenger came without being ridiculed.

studies.applyIt: Learn three ayat by heart this month. Not a whole surah, and not because memorising earns anything: choose three you already half know and get them exact, in order, without looking. The pledge in this passage has been kept through ordinary people doing precisely that. You will also find you notice them in recitation for the rest of your life.

studies.title: A Gateway In The Sky
studies.meaning: The most extreme sign imaginable is granted hypothetically. A door opens in the sky and they climb through it, and the passage supplies their reaction: our eyes are being blocked, in fact we have been bewitched. Commentators note that both halves of that reply are explanations, and that the second is stronger than the first, since it dismisses not one perception but the whole faculty. The following verses then describe the sky itself as set with constellations and guarded, which is the standing arrangement they would have been passing through.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the objectors' demand for angels and the statement that earlier peoples mocked their messengers too. The audience had asked for specific signs, and other surahs list them: a spring made to gush, a house of gold, an ascent into the sky. This passage takes the largest of those requests and answers it before it is granted.

keyTerms.note: The verb for going up by degrees, sharing a root with the word for a stairway. It describes a gradual climb rather than a sudden vision, so the hypothetical gives them all the time they could want.
The lexicographers give both dammed up, as water is stopped, and made intoxicated. Either way the claim is that the instrument has failed, which is what the objection needs in order to work.

The word also means fortified towers, and both senses were current. Placed beside the guarding described next, the fortress sense turns the sky into a structure with defences rather than an open expanse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Soothsayers in Arabia claimed access to news from above, and the culture had a working account of how it arrived: something listened at the edge of the unseen and passed fragments down. The shooting stars everyone saw at night were part of that picture. When this passage speaks of a guarded sky and a pursuing flame, it is engaging a cosmology its audience already held rather than introducing one.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran presses this argument in several forms. One passage says that if a book on parchment had been sent down and they had touched it with their hands, they would still have called it plain magic. Another says that even seeing lumps of the sky falling they would call it a mass of clouds. In each case a different sense is granted and dismissed by the objector.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a move that no evidence can survive: doubting the instrument rather than the datum. Once perception itself is suspect, every possible sign has an answer waiting, and the argument becomes unfalsifiable from the inside. That is why the surah stops asking for belief on evidential grounds after this point. What follows instead is a description of the world as it actually is, offered to whoever will take it.

crossReferences.why: Says a book they could touch with their hands would still have been called plain magic.
Has them explain away falling pieces of the sky as nothing more than gathered clouds.
States the same conclusion, that every sign coming would not move those already settled.

studies.applyIt: Notice the last time you dismissed something by questioning the source rather than the claim. The study was funded by someone, the person had a motive, the account was biased. Sometimes that is exactly right. Try separating the two questions once this week and answering the claim on its own, whatever you conclude about the source.

studies.title: All Things In Measure
studies.meaning: Attention moves from the guarded sky down to the ground in one step. The earth is spread out, weights are set into it, and everything growing there is described as proportioned. Then livelihoods are named, and the sentence adds a group easy to miss: creatures for whom you are not the providers. Commentators take this as covering dependants and animals alike, everything living off an arrangement nobody present set up. The passage lists provision as part of the structure rather than as a separate favour.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the objectors are shown explaining away a gateway in the sky. The surah turns from what they will not accept to what is already in front of them. This move from sky to earth to sustenance recurs across the Quran, and here it introduces a longer passage about stores, winds and water that follows.

keyTerms.note: The verb for extending something, as a cloth is unrolled or a rope drawn out. It describes the earth as it is met by someone standing on it, which is how the Quran usually speaks of the ground.
From the root for a ship riding at anchor. The word does not mean mountain but something that holds steady, so the image is of weights set to keep a spread surface from shifting.
A passive form from the verb to weigh on a balance. It says what grows was measured before it appeared, which makes the vegetation itself the record of a calculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weighing was the daily business of a market town. Grain, dates, silver and incense all moved by balance, and the honesty of a merchant was judged by his weights, which were checked and sometimes disputed publicly. Describing what grows from the ground as weighed out borrowed the most trusted instrument in Mecca and applied it to something no one had thought of measuring.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran repeatedly names creatures that carry no provision of their own and are fed nonetheless, once saying that many a creature does not carry its sustenance and that God provides for them and for you. Another passage states that there is no moving creature on earth whose sustenance is not upon God, and that He knows where it lives and where it rests.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is presented as an aspect of design rather than as charity added afterwards. The earth is spread, steadied and planted in measure, and livelihoods are simply the next item on the same list. That has a consequence for how a person reads their own supply: it arrives through an arrangement that predates them. Naming those they do not provide for extends the point past the household, since the same structure feeds what nobody is responsible for.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sequence, the earth spread with mountains and rivers, as signs for those who reflect.
Names creatures that carry no provision, and says God provides for them and for you alike.
States that no moving creature's sustenance is anywhere but with God, recorded in a clear book.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you will eat today and trace it back three steps: who moved it, who grew it, what weather it needed. Stop when you reach something nobody arranged. The ayah puts provision inside the structure of the world rather than beside it, and tracing a single item is the shortest way to feel that.

studies.title: The Storehouses Of Everything
studies.meaning: Two claims about supply. Everything that exists has its stores with God, and what comes down arrives in a known measure, so scarcity and abundance are both quantities rather than accidents. Then the mechanism: winds are sent that make things fertile, water falls, you are given it to drink. The closing clause is the sting. You are not the ones who store it. Commentators note the ayah gives people the drinking and withholds the keeping, which is exactly the division everyone experiences and rarely states.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage moving from the sky to the earth to what sustains life on it. Mecca had no river and no farmland, and its water came from wells in a dry valley. An audience in that setting did not need the point about storage explained; nobody there had ever held a reserve of rain, and the whole city's water security rested on sources they had not made.

keyTerms.note: Plural of the room where valuables are kept under lock. Saying every single thing has such a store with God turns supply into something released rather than something that happens to appear.
From the root for measuring and for power. It states that quantity is decided rather than accidental, which applies as much to a year of little rain as to a year of much.
The word occurs once in the Quran. It is used of winds that carry what makes things bear, and the commentators connect it to the pollination of palms and to clouds made heavy with water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date palms had to be pollinated by hand or by wind, and every farmer in the oases knew the season for it and what a failure cost. Water itself could not be hoarded in a hot valley; skins leaked, cisterns evaporated, and wells were shared under agreements that took generations to settle. A Meccan household lived on a supply it could use but never accumulate.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for winds that make things bear appears only once in the whole Quran. The Quran describes winds elsewhere in the same role without this term, saying that God sends the winds which stir clouds and drive them to dead ground, reviving it. Only this passage names the winds themselves by a word taken from fertility.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things people find hard to hold together are stated in one breath. Supply is unlimited at the source, since everything has its stores, and strictly measured at delivery. That rules out both the anxiety that there is not enough and the assumption that more is always available. Denying human beings the role of storekeeper then removes the last illusion of control, since what can be drunk today cannot be secured for a decade.

crossReferences.why: States the same authority over supply, spreading bounty for some and reducing it for others.
Asks who sent down the water you drink, and notes it could have been made undrinkable.
Describes the winds driving clouds to dead land and uses the reviving as an image of resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you try to stockpile against the future. Money is obvious; more often it is energy, goodwill, or a sense of being ahead. Ask honestly how much of it actually keeps. The ayah grants you the drinking and denies you the storing, and most of what we hoard turns out to work the same way.

studies.title: And We Are The Inheritors
studies.meaning: Giving life and causing death are stated together, and then a title is added that reframes both: We are the ones who remain. Commentators explain the inheritance as what happens when every owner has gone and everything reverts. The next verse says those who go ahead and those who lag behind are equally known, which the classical readings take variously as earlier and later generations, or as those first and last in ranks and in obedience. Then the gathering, and then the clay.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage that has moved from the guarded sky through the earth and its provision to the human being. The surah is building its case from structure rather than from argument at this stage. No occasion is reported. The audience acknowledged a creator and disputed the gathering, which is why these four verses put creation and resurrection inside a single sequence.

keyTerms.note: The word for those who receive what an owner leaves. Used of God it means what stays when everything else has gone, so the term describes permanence through the vocabulary of succession.
Occurring once in the Quran, paired here with its opposite. The classical readings run from earlier and later generations to those forward and behind in rank, and the sources keep the range.
Clay dried to the point where it rings when struck. The word appears four times in the Quran, three of them in this surah, and it names a material both fragile and resonant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance disputes were among the most bitter matters an Arabian clan handled. Herds, wells and standing were divided when a man died, and the arguments could run for years and reshape a family permanently. Everyone understood that possession is temporary and that everything eventually passes to someone else. This passage takes that certainty and asks who is at the end of the chain.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for clay dried until it rings appears four times in the Quran and three of those are in this surah, in verses twenty-six, twenty-eight and thirty-three. The third occurrence is spoken by Iblis, who repeats the description of the material back to God as his reason for refusing. The phrase is used as a boast about material and as an insult about it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming God as the one who remains puts every possession into a chain that has an end. That is a claim about time rather than about ownership: things are not merely lent, they are on their way somewhere. Setting this beside the knowledge of who goes ahead and who lags behind also removes the anonymity of a crowd. Whatever the gathering is, it is not described as a mass event but as one where each position is already known.

crossReferences.why: States the same inheritance directly, of the earth and everyone on it, with the return to Him.
Puts the same idea as a contrast, everyone upon it perishing while the face of your Lord remains.
Traces the making of the human being from clay through its stages to a new creature.

studies.applyIt: Pick up something in your home you would be sorry to lose and ask who will have it in eighty years. Not to make yourself gloomy; simply to place the object correctly. The ayah does not ask you to stop caring for what you own. It asks you to know where in the chain you are standing.

studies.title: Formed, Then Breathed Into
studies.meaning: Two materials are named before anything happens. The unseen beings were made earlier from a scorching fire, and the human being from dried clay out of dark mud. Then the announcement to the angels and the condition attached: when I have shaped him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him. Commentators are careful that the breathing is not a division of God's own being but an honour conferred, and they note that the command follows the breath rather than the clay.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This scene appears in several surahs with different portions preserved, and the Quran assumes the outline is known. Here it is placed after a long passage on the sky, the earth and provision, so the making of the human being arrives as the last item in a description of how things are, rather than as a separate story.

keyTerms.note: The second word names a searing wind that penetrates the pores. The compound describes fire at its most invasive rather than its brightest, which is the material assigned to the unseen beings.
The first word is black mud that has stood; the second means either poured into a mould or altered by time. Both senses are recorded, and either way the material has a history before the shaping.
The possessive marks honour rather than composition, as the Quran elsewhere calls a house My house. The commentators hold that nothing of God's essence is divided or transferred by the phrase.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Potters worked with exactly this sequence, and everyone had watched it. River mud was gathered, left to stand until it darkened and grew workable, shaped by hand, then dried until it rang under a knuckle. A vessel at that stage was finished in form and still useless. The account borrows a craft its audience knew intimately and stops the process one step before the end.
studies.didYouKnow: This scene is told in at least six surahs and each keeps different details. One records the angels asking why a creature who would shed blood should be placed on earth, and the teaching of the names. Another gives the material as clay without the mud. This surah is the only one that names the material three separate times in the space of eight verses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Honour is located in what was added rather than in the material, which is the point Iblis will miss in the next verses. Clay is not dignified and the passage does not pretend otherwise; the command to bow comes only after the breathing. That sets a pattern for how the Quran speaks about human worth throughout, as something conferred rather than possessed, and it explains why an argument from material misses the case entirely.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sequence, forming, breathing and the command, and then the refusal and its reason.
Preserves the angels' question about a creature who would shed blood, and the teaching of the names.
Joins the same breathing to the giving of hearing, sight and understanding, and to thankfulness.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you find it hard to respect, and separate the two questions this passage separates. What are they made of, in terms of behaviour and circumstance, and what was put into them that had nothing to do with any of that. You do not have to like them. Just notice which of the two your judgement is resting on.

studies.title: He Refused To Be Among Them
studies.meaning: Everyone bowed, and the exception is stated twice over: he refused, and he would not be among those bowing. The question put to him is about company rather than obedience, asking what kept him from being with them. His answer repeats the material description word for word from the announcement, which the commentators read as an argument from substance: he will not bow to something made of that. The reply names the consequence without arguing back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed to a people whose objection to the message was also partly about rank. Their complaint was that revelation had come to an ordinary man from among them, which is an argument about material in a different form. The scene is told across several surahs, and this version keeps the exchange short and gives most of its space to the refusal itself.

keyTerms.note: A blunt verb of refusal with no explanation attached. Placing it before any reasoning shows the position was taken first, and the argument about clay arrives afterwards as its justification.
A participle naming a group rather than an act, and the question asks why he was not among them. What is being refused is described as membership, which is a different failure from disobedience.
From the root for stoning or pelting something away. It names expulsion by force rather than a title, and the same word described the devils repelled from the sky earlier in this surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Precedence was visible and constantly negotiated in Arabian gatherings. Where a man sat, when he spoke, and whether he rose for someone were public statements about rank, and refusing an expected courtesy was a serious act done in front of witnesses. The scene here would have read as that kind of moment: not a private disagreement but a refusal made in an assembly where everyone else complied.
studies.didYouKnow: The refusal is reported in several surahs and the stated reason is consistent wherever it is given: I am better than he, You created me from fire and him from clay. In this surah the reason is phrased differently, repeating back the exact description of the material that had been used in the announcement, so the objection quotes the very words it is answering.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pride is diagnosed as a comparison of origins. The refusal is not a denial of God's authority, since the speaker addresses God directly throughout and never disputes His right to command. What is disputed is the worth of the one being honoured, judged by what he is made of. That is why the passage placed the breathing before the command: the case for honour was never the clay, and the argument about clay was therefore never an answer.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reason in its usual form, better than he, created from fire against mud.
Adds God's question about whether he was too proud, and the same answer about the two materials.
Records the refusal as a question, whether he should bow to one created from mud.

studies.applyIt: Notice one person you would find it hard to take instruction from because of what they are rather than what they said. Younger, less qualified, from somewhere you rate lower. Take one piece of their advice this week on its own merits. The argument from material is the oldest one there is, and it is usually still doing its work quietly.

studies.title: Until The Appointed Time
studies.meaning: A curse is pronounced until the Day of Recompense, and then something unexpected happens. The one expelled makes a request, and it is granted. Commentators note the exact wording of both sides: he asks for time until the day people are raised, and the answer gives him time until the day of the known appointment, which is not quite the same phrase. The sources discuss the difference at length without settling it. What is not in doubt is that a request from an enemy was answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of the scene that follows the making of the human being. The exchange appears in several surahs with slight variations in the wording of the request and the grant. Its placement here matters: this surah has just told its audience that no community is destroyed except at its written term, and the reprieve granted here belongs to the same principle.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to drive away and exclude. It names removal from mercy rather than an imprecation uttered, which is why it can be stated as a fact with a stated duration.
From the verb for looking, in a form meaning to give someone a period before acting. It is the standard word for extending a debtor's term, so the request uses ordinary commercial language.

A moment fixed and known, though known to whom is left open. The commentators note that the answer does not simply repeat the request's wording, and they preserve the question rather than resolving it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Extending a term was a familiar transaction. A creditor could grant a debtor more time, and the extension was stated with a limit rather than left open, because an unbounded delay was no agreement at all. Everyone understood that a granted period is not a pardon. The vocabulary of this exchange comes straight out of that practice, including the request and the bounded answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this exchange in at least three surahs. In two of them the request is for respite until the day people are raised, and the answer grants respite until the day of the known time, using a phrase that does not repeat the request. Classical commentators noticed the mismatch and discussed whether the two days are the same, without reaching a common answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A request made by an enemy in open rebellion is granted, which says something uncomfortable and important about how the world is arranged. The interval that follows is the whole of human history, and it exists by permission rather than by oversight. Bounding it also matters. Everything that happens in this stretch of time is happening inside a term that was set at the beginning and is known at least to the one who set it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same expulsion and the same request and grant, in almost identical wording.
Records the request and the answer with the same phrase about the day of the known time.
States earlier in this surah that no community outruns or delays its own appointed term.

studies.applyIt: Consider that the time you are living in is described here as a granted interval rather than a default state. Not to frighten yourself. Simply pick one thing today that you would do differently if you took that literally, and do that one thing. The passage treats the whole stretch as an extension with a term attached.

studies.title: I Will Make It Look Good
studies.meaning: The stated method is not force and not deception about facts. It is making things on earth look attractive, and the commentators note how modest a power that describes. Nothing is created, nothing is compelled, and no new option is introduced; the surface of what is already there is adjusted. The oath that follows extends the claim to everyone, and the passage lets it stand unchallenged for one verse before the exception arrives.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the reprieve is granted. The surah has just spent several verses describing a world made in measure and provided for, and this declaration follows directly. Its placement suggests the danger is not a rival creation but a distorted view of the one that exists, which the surah develops as it goes on.

keyTerms.note: From a root for losing the way and for a mind gone wrong. The speaker attributes his own refusal to God, which the commentators note is the first move of a position that will not examine itself.
An intensive verb for adorning something, sharing a root with the word for finery. The work described is cosmetic, applied to the appearance of things rather than to the things themselves.
The stated arena, and it is a limit as much as a scope. Nothing is claimed beyond this world, so the whole enterprise is confined to the interval that was just granted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Traders knew the difference between goods and their presentation. Dates were arranged with the best fruit on top, cloth was shown in a particular light, and a camel could be walked in a way that hid a defect for as long as the buyer was watching. Nobody in that market thought the presentation changed the goods. They knew it changed the sale.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this word for making deeds look attractive in many places, and it does not always name the same agent. Several passages attribute the beautifying to Satan, one to God as a matter of how things are left to seem, and one asks about the man whose evil deed has been made to look good so that he regards it as good. The verb stays constant while the framing shifts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The power claimed here is remarkably limited and therefore worth taking seriously. Nothing is added to the world, and nothing is taken from the person's ability to choose; what changes is how something appears at the moment of deciding. That places the whole struggle inside perception, which is why the Quran keeps returning to attention and reflection. The blaming of God in the first clause also stands as a warning about how such a position sustains itself.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same beautifying at work in a specific battle, followed by immediate abandonment.
Asks about the man whose evil deed was made attractive so that he considers it good.
Joins the hardening of hearts to deeds made to appear good, when calamity failed to humble them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you made that felt obviously right at the time and looked different a week later. Nothing changed except the framing. Before your next significant choice, write one sentence describing it in the plainest words you can find, with no reasons attached. That single move undoes most of what this verse describes.

studies.title: Brothers On Facing Couches
studies.meaning: The description is built from removals as much as from gifts. Gardens and springs are named, then entry in peace and safety, and then the striking clause: whatever ill feeling was in their chests is drawn out. The commentators take this as the removal of grudges carried from this life, so that people who had reason to resent each other sit facing one another as kin. Fatigue is denied, and expulsion is denied. The passage closes with an instruction to inform God's servants of two of His names.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage answers the section immediately before it, in which Satan is granted power only over those who follow him and Hell is described with seven gates. This is the counterweight, given in the same measured tone. No particular occasion is reported. The surah belongs to the middle Meccan years, when the small community was under social pressure and the promise of a place where no one can be expelled had a sharp edge.

keyTerms.note: The word names a hidden grudge lodged in the chest, not open hostility. The root is used of a hand bound to the neck, which gives the sense of something knotted and held rather than expressed.

A verb of pulling something out by force, used of drawing a bucket from a well or a weapon from its sheath. The grudges are extracted rather than forgotten, which implies they were real and lodged deep.

Bodily exhaustion from effort, distinct from grief or boredom. Denying it addresses a specific fear about eternity, that even rest becomes wearying, and the second denial answers the other fear, of being sent away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia were inherited property. A killing in one generation obliged the next to answer it, and clans could carry a grievance for decades, reciting the names of the dead in poetry so no one forgot. Sitting facing someone was a posture of trust, which is why guests were seated in view of each other. To promise that the grudges themselves would be pulled out was to promise something no truce had ever managed.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about drawing rancour from the chest occurs twice in the Quran, here and in a passage on the people of the garden in another surah, with almost identical wording. Notice also that the final ayat pair a name of forgiveness with a warning about punishment in the very next line, a balance the commentators treat as characteristic of this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Paradise is described as a repair of relationships, not only as a reward. Something is taken out of the people themselves before they are seated together, which says that the obstacle to peace was internal and that God treats it directly. The passage then moves from description to address, instructing that the servants be told what God is, and the naming comes as news to be delivered rather than as a conclusion the hearer must reach alone.

crossReferences.why: The same removal of rancour, there followed by the words of those who arrive.
A prayer of later believers asking that no rancour toward earlier ones remain in their hearts.
Also denies fatigue in the garden, in the words of those already inside it.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind one person you have not forgiven. You do not have to contact them, and you do not have to feel differently. Just try, once, to describe what happened without the word they in an accusing position. Notice how hard that is. This passage says the grudge is something removed rather than argued away, and noticing its weight is where that begins.

studies.title: Do Not Stretch Your Eyes
studies.meaning: Three instructions in one breath, each addressing a different pressure. The first forbids a lingering look at the comfort granted to groups among the opponents; the verb suggests stretching the gaze rather than glancing. The second forbids grief over them, which the commentators read as sorrow at their refusal rather than at their wealth. The third asks for gentleness towards believers, using an image of a bird lowering its wing over its young.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, late in the period there. The ayah directly follows the mention of the seven oft-repeated verses and the Grand Quran, so the sequence is deliberate: you have been given this, do not look at that. Opponents in Mecca included some of the wealthiest families in the city, and the small community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was drawn largely from those without such backing. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of extending a rope or a shadow. Applied to the eyes it describes a look that keeps going, so what is discouraged is dwelling rather than seeing.
An intensive form of a verb meaning to furnish with goods for a time. The word itself carries a term limit, so the very phrase describing their wealth marks it as temporary.
A bird lowers its wing to shelter its young and raises it to threaten. The idiom means to make yourself approachable and safe, and the same image appears in the command about ageing parents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was visible in a small number of specific things: the number of camels in a caravan share, a house near the sanctuary, clients who owed you, daughters married into other clans. There was no way not to notice who had them. Meanwhile the believers included freed slaves and men who had been disowned. Telling one group not to look at the other was addressing a daily, physical arrangement of the town.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah before this one refers to seven repeated verses, which most commentators identify as the opening surah, recited in every unit of prayer. Setting that beside the wealth of opponents is a deliberate comparison of holdings. The wing image recurs twice more in the Quran, once about followers and once about ageing parents.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Envy is treated as a problem of attention before it is a problem of desire, which is why the instruction concerns the eyes. The passage also separates two griefs that often merge: sorrow at another's refusal of guidance is real and is still set aside, because responsibility for their response is not being carried. What remains after both prohibitions is not resignation but a redirection, since the final clause gives somewhere for the freed attention to go.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction almost exactly, adding that your Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
Gives the same command about lowering the wing, there over those who follow.
Tells the Prophet to stay with those who call on their Lord and not to look past them.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time your eyes stay on someone else's life for longer than a glance: a photo, a car, a house someone posted. Do not argue with yourself about it. Just close the app or look away, and then do one small thing for a person who is actually near you. The ayah puts those two moves side by side for a reason.
